mentions.quote: This holy kṛcchra penance was prescribed by Aṅgiras himself, and by learned knowers of dharma, for the destruction of secondary sins.
This holy kṛcchra penance was prescribed by Aṅgiras himself. Beginning with the Praṇava, it is remembered by the name vajra.
Thus the Smṛti of Aṅgiras.

entities.description: The ancient Vedic sage Aṅgiras, presented as the divine author and lawgiver of this Dharmaśāstra who personally prescribed the kṛcchra penance.
entities.justification: Aṅgiras is named as the personal prescriber of penances and the text closes with attribution to his Smṛti, identifying him as the founding authority of the entire work.

mentions.quote: I shall now declare the exception which was stated by Manu in ancient times.
the penance should be known as the same as for a cow; thus said the blessed Manu.

entities.description: The primordial lawgiver Manu, cited as an ancient authority on dietary exceptions and penance equivalences for animal-killing.
entities.justification: Manu is invoked twice as an external authority whose rulings on food prohibitions and penance tariffs the Aṅgiras text explicitly endorses.

mentions.quote: The chastiser of those with hidden sins is Yama, the son of Vivasvat.
The Guru, the king, or Yama, when he chastises according to dharma, is freed from sin.

entities.description: Yama, god of death and cosmic justice, identified as the son of Vivasvat, who chastises those with concealed sins beyond the reach of human authority.
entities.justification: Yama is placed in a triadic authority structure alongside the Guru and king, marking his role as the ultimate enforcer of moral law for hidden transgressions.

mentions.quote: The chastiser of those with hidden sins is Yama, the son of Vivasvat.

entities.description: Vivasvat, the solar deity, named as the father of Yama in the standard Vedic genealogy.
entities.justification: Vivasvat is mentioned solely to identify Yama's divine parentage, grounding Yama's cosmic authority in solar/Vedic mythology.

mentions.quote: Four or three Brahmins who know the Vedas, keep the sacred fires, are well-established, and have determined what is to be done and not to be done
For minor acts, this assembly is small; for medium acts, it is medium. For the consideration of great sins, it is a hundred.
The strength of the assembly is in the rule, and the strength of the rule is in the assembly.
For great sins, the assembly is a hundred; for the greatest, a thousand. For secondary sins, fifty.

entities.description: The formal assembly of qualified Brahmins constituted to hear confessions, deliberate on sins, and prescribe penances; its size scales with the severity of the offense.
entities.justification: The pariṣad is the central institutional mechanism of this text, elaborated across multiple chapters with detailed rules for its composition, authority, and procedure.

mentions.quote: By birth, body, and knowledge, by conduct and by scripture, and by dharma as prescribed, Brahminhood is ordained.
Brahmins are the field; Brahmins are the deity. By the grace of Brahmins, the sun shines in the sky.
There is no field equal to a Brahmin, no fire equal to a Brahmin. There is no rule above a Brahmin, no god beyond a Brahmin.

entities.description: The Brahmin class, positioned as the supreme social-religious group whose knowledge of Dharmaśāstra, Veda, and conduct makes them the proper arbiters of penance and ritual purity.
entities.justification: Brahmins are the institutional and cosmic center of this text: they staff the pariṣad, prescribe penances, and are declared superior to all other humans and even gods.

mentions.quote: That fire-keeping Brahmin who accepts gifts from a Śūdra attains the same state as the eaters and goes to an animal birth.
He who, while studying the Veda, eats a Śūdra's food, the fruit of his Veda goes to the Śūdra, and he himself attains the state of a Śūdra.
A Śūdra is purified by time, being devoted to the welfare of cows and Brahmins, or by charity, or by fasts.
mentions.role: subject of a modified penance regime

entities.description: The lowest of the four varṇas, whose food and gifts are treated as ritually contaminating for twice-born; yet also a subject of penance through a modified dharmic path.
entities.justification: The Śūdra appears throughout chapters 8–9 as the paradigmatic source of ritual pollution through food contact, while chapter 5 also addresses their penance regime.

mentions.quote: Having bathed with his clothes on, observing silence, with wet garments, and with a concentrated mind, a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya should approach.
A Brahmin for Brahmins, a reader for Kṣatriyas, and the questioner for Vaiśyas—they are remembered as the givers of the rule.
mentions.role: one of three upper varṇas in judicial context

entities.description: The warrior-ruler class, who are subject to the pariṣad penance procedure but require a Brahmin intermediary to function within the assembly structure.
entities.justification: Kṣatriyas are addressed alongside Brahmins and Vaiśyas in the procedural sections on approaching the assembly and the composition of the prescribing body.

mentions.quote: If one strikes a cow with a stick and kills it, a penance of double the govrata is ordained.
the killer of cows—these four are proclaimed as fallen.
That cow-killer who follows the cows according to this rule is freed from the sin of cow-killing.
mentions.role: ritual focus of the cow-killing penance

mentions.quote: A cow that is sick, accursed, or in fear of thieves, tigers, and other dangers, or has fallen or is stuck in mud—he should rescue it with all his might.

entities.description: The cow, the most sacred animal in this text, whose killing constitutes a major sin requiring a dedicated two-month penance (govrata), and whose protection and service are central duties.
entities.justification: Chapters 10 and 11 are devoted almost entirely to cow-injury and cow-killing penances, making the cow the primary animal figure of this window.

mentions.quote: The Guru is the chastiser of the self-controlled; the king is the chastiser of the wicked.
The Guru, the king, or Yama, when he chastises according to dharma, is freed from sin.
a defiler of the Guru's bed

entities.description: The Guru (spiritual teacher/preceptor), ranked as the first of three legitimate authorities who may chastise, and whose bed-defilement constitutes one of the five great sins.
entities.justification: The Guru appears as the apex of the triadic chastisement hierarchy (Guru → king → Yama) and as a protected figure whose violation defines a mahāpātaka.

mentions.quote: The king shines by truth; the sun shines by truth.
The Guru is the chastiser of the self-controlled; the king is the chastiser of the wicked.
The assembly for kings is remembered as double that of Brahmins.

entities.description: The king (rājan), who shines by truth, serves as the second tier in the triadic chastisement hierarchy, requires a larger pariṣad assembly than Brahmins, and relies on a Brahmin intermediary.
entities.justification: The king is invoked as both a cosmological emblem of truth and a functional legal authority whose penance procedure is more elaborate than that of Brahmins.

mentions.quote: A Brahmin-killer, a gold-thief, a liquor-drinker, a defiler of the Guru's bed, and he who associates with these—he is the fifth; these five are the great sinners.

entities.description: The canonical five categories of mahāpātaka (great sin): Brahmin-killing, gold-theft, liquor-drinking, defilement of the Guru's bed, and association with any of the four.
entities.justification: The text provides a verbatim enumeration of the pañca-mahāpātaka, a standard classificatory group in Dharmaśāstra literature, as the framework for the most severe penance prescriptions.

mentions.quote: The killer of a woman or a man, the defiler of a maiden, and the killer of cows—these four are proclaimed as fallen.

entities.description: The patita class: those who have committed irremediable sins (killing women, men, defilement of a maiden, cow-killing) and are declared ritually outcast.
entities.justification: The text formally enumerates the patita category immediately after the mahāpātaka list, establishing the taxonomy of the most severe transgressions.

mentions.quote: Having committed a sin, one should not hide it; being hidden, it grows. Whether it is small or great, one should confess it to the knowers of dharma.
Thus permitted by them, he should state the whole truth. When the matter has been confessed, he who has the purpose should be dismissed.

themes.justification: Chapters 2–3 open with the imperative to confess sin openly and the ritual procedure for approaching the assembly, making public acknowledgment of transgression the prerequisite for penance.

themes.topic: Truth (satya) as cosmic and moral foundation

mentions.quote: The king shines by truth; the sun shines by truth. Fire shines by truth; everything is established in truth.
The three worlds—earth, atmosphere, and heaven—are also established in truth. For us and for all, truth alone is the supreme path.
If you speak the truth, you will surely attain happiness. But if you are seized by untruth, you will never be purified.

themes.justification: Chapter 3 elevates satya (truth) to a cosmic principle underpinning all three worlds, the sun, fire, and kingship, making truthful confession not merely a legal but an ontological requirement.

themes.topic: Composition, qualification, and authority of the penance-prescribing assembly

mentions.quote: Four or three Brahmins who know the Vedas, keep the sacred fires, are well-established, and have determined what is to be done and not to be done.
For minor acts, this assembly is small; for medium acts, it is medium. For the consideration of great sins, it is a hundred.
Those Brahmins who are beyond this, who are merely bearers of the name, have no status as an assembly, even if they are thousands.

themes.justification: Chapters 4–5 are devoted to specifying which Brahmins qualify for assembly membership and what quorum is required by sin-severity, making institutional competence the central concern.

themes.topic: Transfer and dissolution of sin through penance and assembly

mentions.quote: The sin of the performer, which is being appeased by dharma according to scripture, goes entirely to the prescriber; I shall tell you the parts.
It goes neither to the doer nor to the assembly member. Through contact with the wind and the sun's rays, it dissolves like water.
Burned by the triple fire of their wisdom, it is destroyed; of this there is no doubt, just as frost is by the sight of the sun.

themes.justification: Chapter 6 works through a subtle problem of moral bookkeeping: when a well-constituted assembly prescribes penance correctly, sin is dissolved cosmically rather than transferred to anyone, an implicit concern about the assembly's own liability.

themes.topic: Ritual pollution from Śūdra food and the graduated purity of twice-born

mentions.quote: That fire-keeping Brahmin who accepts gifts from a Śūdra attains the same state as the eaters and goes to an animal birth.
He who, while studying the Veda, eats a Śūdra's food, the fruit of his Veda goes to the Śūdra, and he himself attains the state of a Śūdra.
He who eats a Śūdra's food continuously for six months becomes a Śūdra while still alive, and after death is born as a dog.

themes.justification: Chapter 8 develops an elaborate taxonomy of food-pollution from Śūdra sources, with escalating consequences from ritual degradation to rebirth as a dog, encoding caste hierarchy through alimentary rules.

themes.topic: The sacred status of cows and the penance regime for cow-harm

mentions.quote: If one strikes a cow with a stick and kills it, a penance of double the govrata is ordained.
He should follow the cows daily and always drink their dust.
That cow-killer who follows the cows according to this rule is freed from the sin of cow-killing.

themes.justification: Chapters 10–11 develop the most detailed penance in the window, the govrata, in which the cow-killer must literally live as a cow for two months, encoding the cow's supreme sacred value.

themes.topic: Supremacy of Brahmins as cosmic field and divine mediators

mentions.quote: Brahmins are the field; Brahmins are the deity. By the grace of Brahmins, the sun shines in the sky.
There is no field equal to a Brahmin, no fire equal to a Brahmin. There is no rule above a Brahmin, no god beyond a Brahmin.
In a Brahmin are all the gods, and he is the god of gods.

themes.justification: Chapter 12 closes the work with an extended doxology of Brahmin supremacy that goes beyond procedural dharma to stake a metaphysical claim: Brahmins contain all gods and their mouths are superior to the Agnihotra fire.

themes.topic: Gradation of penance by varṇa, age, sex, and intentionality

mentions.quote: For women who have sinned intentionally, half the penance should be prescribed.
For one who has passed eighty years of age, the full penance is reduced by half.
What is done unintentionally is doubled if done intentionally.

themes.justification: The text implicitly encodes a complex jurisprudential logic of moral mitigating factors—intentionality doubles guilt, while age below 12 or above 80 and female sex halve it—never stated as a general principle but consistently applied.

themes.topic: The kṛcchra penance and the vajra vow as instruments of purification

mentions.quote: This holy kṛcchra penance was prescribed by Aṅgiras himself. Beginning with the Praṇava, it is remembered by the name vajra.
This penance is ordained for those who are joined with sin. Those joined with great sins are purified by three years of it.
He should recite the Sāvitrī or the Vyāhṛtis eight thousand times, placing Oṃkāra at the beginning.

themes.justification: Chapter 12 describes the signature kṛcchra-vajra penance of this text, attributed to Aṅgiras himself, which combines recitation, dietary austerity, and physical posture into a sustained purificatory regime.

citations.quote: I shall now declare the exception which was stated by Manu in ancient times.
citations.justification: Manu is explicitly named as an ancient authority whose ruling on Śūdra food exceptions the Aṅgiras text invokes and defers to.

citations.quote: the penance should be known as the same as for a cow; thus said the blessed Manu.
citations.justification: Manu is cited again as the originating authority for the ruling that penance for killing listed animals equals the cow-killing penance.
